title: Manoj Bajpayee Is Playing the Man Who Saved India From Bankruptcy. The Tickets Cost What They Did in 1990.
excerpt: Governor reimagines the balance-of-payments crisis with Amit Trivedi's score, Javed Akhtar's lyrics, and the boldest ticket-pricing stunt Bollywood has tried in years.
body:
There's a moment in the trailer for Governor where Manoj Bajpayee sits across from a room full of bureaucrats and says, quietly, as if he's already exhausted by everything that's coming: "If I fail, India fails."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Mvm0bRY0Qyg

It lands. Not because the line is clever, but because anyone who knows what happened to India in 1990 knows he isn't exaggerating.

Governor is set against the backdrop of India's most severe financial crisis — the balance-of-payments emergency triggered by the Gulf War, when the country's foreign exchange reserves dipped so low that India had barely enough to cover two weeks of imports. The man tasked with keeping the country from defaulting was S. Venkitaramanan, the RBI Governor whose quiet, unglamorous decisions over a matter of months helped steer India toward the economic liberalization of 1991 — the single most consequential policy shift in modern Indian history.

Bajpayee plays Venkitaramanan, and if there's an actor alive in Hindi cinema who can make a man behind a desk feel like the most dangerous person in the room, it's him. The film is directed by Chinmay Mandlekar, the Marathi cinema powerhouse behind Har Har Mahadev and Dharmaveer, and if you've seen his work, you know he doesn't do small. The screenplay, co-written by Suvendu Bhattacharyjee, Saurabh Bharat, Ravi Asrani, and producer Vipul Amrutlal Shah, leans into the political chess of the crisis — bureaucratic turf wars, institutional resistance, and the slow-building dread of a sovereign default.

The supporting cast adds texture. Adah Sharma plays Aditi Verma, a reporter trying to pry open a story the government would rather bury. Madhoo — yes, Roja's Madhoo — returns as Vandita in a role that reportedly grounds the emotional stakes of the film in something more personal than GDP numbers. Noushad Mohamed Kunju plays C. Rangarajan, the RBI deputy who would later become Governor himself and architect of India's inflation targeting.

"There was a time when there were no malls" — Manoj Bajpayee, on what Governor reveals to Gen Z about pre-liberalization India

The creative pedigree is stacked. Javed Akhtar wrote the lyrics — at 81, the man still can't resist a project that smells like history. The music is by Amit Trivedi, whose range from Dev.D's acid-folk to Lootera's melancholy means the score could go anywhere. The CBFC has cleared it UA 13+, with a runtime of 122 minutes — tight for a political thriller, which is a good sign. Nobody needs a three-hour lecture about forex reserves.

But the real conversation-starter is the marketing. The makers announced that the first 25,000 tickets on BookMyShow will be priced at 1990s rates. That's not a typo. In a month where Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey IMAX tickets are touching ₹3,000 in Pune, Governor is offering seats at whatever a movie cost when Doordarshan was still the main competition. It's a gimmick, sure. But it's a brilliant one — it makes you Google what things actually cost in 1990, which is exactly the curiosity the film wants to trigger.

For the diaspora, this is personal. The 1991 liberalization didn't just change India's economy — it created the India that produced you. Every NRI engineer in Silicon Valley, every finance professional in the City of London, every doctor who matched at a US residency program — the opportunity pipeline that made all of that possible was built on the rubble of the crisis this film depicts. Venkitaramanan's decisions didn't just save India from bankruptcy. They opened the doors that an entire generation of Indians walked through to build lives abroad. This film serves as a reminder of those pivotal moments that shaped the lives of countless NRIs, reinforcing family ties and professional networks that span continents.

Governor releases on June 12, in what is already Bollywood's most crowded week of 2026. It competes directly with Imtiaz Ali's Main Vaapas Aaunga and Kangana Ranaut's Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata — a trio of films that, taken together, represent three very different chapters of Indian history arriving on the same Friday. The smart money says it won't win the box office race. But it might be the one people remember longest.
